Tune the training
Uses the same photos you labelled, but with the chemist's labels. Any change in accuracy comes from your labelling mistakes.
300
More rounds fit the model more tightly to your labelled photos. Too many and it memorises them instead of learning a general rule.
0.030
Higher values stop the model trusting any single feature too much. That can help with few photos, but too much and it can't learn anything.
0.3
How big a step the model takes each training round. Too small and it barely learns in the rounds it has; too big and it overshoots, so the accuracy curve jumps about. Switching model type puts it back to that model's usual value.
50%
How sure the model must be that solid is left before it calls a photo insoluble. Lower it to catch more insoluble samples, at the cost of more false alarms; raise it and the reverse. Watch “What it got right and wrong”.
6 of 24
The other 18 test photos are 6 each of beakers, conical flasks and round-bottom flasks. The screen is all vials: does a test set like it predict the screen better?

Here the "positive" class is insoluble, because spotting solid is the model's job.

Precision: of the photos the model called insoluble, how many really were? Low precision means false alarms.

Recall: of the photos that really were insoluble, how many did the model catch? Low recall means solid that went unnoticed.

How this model actually works

Every photo is shrunk to 192×192 pixels and turned into a short list of numbers, called features. With spot detectors, the photo is blurred at three sizes and a "blob" filter (built from the second derivatives of brightness) lights up wherever there is a small round shape, such as a particle. Straight lines, such as the glass outline or the liquid surface, barely register. For each spot size the model counts how many pixels light up across the whole photo and across the bottom 40%, giving 24 numbers. With the pixel grid, the photo is averaged into 12×12 squares with a red, green and blue value each: 432 numbers, as in flame test model.

Those numbers feed a logistic regression classifier. It trains by gradient descent right here in your browser: in each training round it nudges one weight per feature to make its guesses agree better with your labels. Regularisation pulls every weight back towards zero. Nothing is pre-recorded, and no photo or label leaves your browser.

The solubility screen

Enter labelling codes: the model trains itself, then runs the screen.
✕ = model disagrees with the key
soluble (dissolved) insoluble paler = less sure Tap a vial to see its photo.

This is a base solubility screen: 11 bases in 4 solvents at 30, 60 and 80 °C, one vial photo for each of the 132 combinations. These photos are messier than the training images, with coloured backgrounds, tilted vials and even a broken one. Your model now predicts every vial. Could it replace a chemist looking at the vials?
